findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring 2026_27 as at Month 4
findings.headline: On-street parking income £0.47m below budget due to demand stabilization post-tariff changes, indicating structural revenue loss
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £0.47m adverse variance on on-street parking income. The council attributes this to 'stabilisation in rates and usage following the pricing changes introduced in 2025/26', indicating that demand has adjusted downward and plateaued at a lower level rather than recovering. Bus lane enforcement and moving traffic contravention income are lower than the prior year but currently in line with budget at £0.00m variance, with improved compliance at Kingston Road offsetting the impact of reduced enforcement hours at Crescent Road. This suggests enforcement income is also stabilizing at lower levels.
findings.matters: Parking income is a discretionary revenue that the council cannot easily grow. A structural reduction in both volume and tariff indicates the council has less flexibility to increase this income stream in future. Combined with other income shortfalls (Land Charges £0.07m, advertising income £0.30m delayed), this points to recurring income volatility.
findings.figures: £0.47m on-street parking adverse variance; rates and usage stabilized at lower levels following 2025/26 pricing changes; enforcement income in line with budget (£0.00m variance)
findings.quote: The main variance in resources is an adverse variance of £0.47m in the on-street parking account. This reflects the stabilisation in rates and usage following the pricing changes introduced in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring 2026_27 as at Month 4
findings.headline: Adult Social Care Care Packages overspending by £0.76m driven by provider cost challenges and £0.3m health partner income shortfall
findings.detail: ASC Care Packages are forecasting a £0.76m overspend. The main driver is market pressure: 'a high number of providers have challenged the uplift awarded for care package costs' and commissioning staff are continuing negotiations with £0.5m in costs estimated pending conclusion. Additionally, health partner income is falling short by 'just under £0.3m' as budgeted amounts exceed what will actually be received, with figures for the previous year only recently confirmed. These pressures persist despite the council's transformation programme, which is helping to manage demand through greater focus on prevention and home support rather than residential placements.
findings.matters: Care provider cost inflation driven by market competition for staff is a structural risk unlikely to be reversed. The health income gap suggests underlying funding misalignment that may persist or worsen. Combined, these represent an ongoing cost pressure that may not be controllable through efficiency measures alone.
findings.figures: £0.76m ASC Care Packages overspend; £0.5m pending provider cost negotiations; £0.3m health income shortfall; 1,600+ adults with long-term care needs supported
findings.quote: Market pressures are the main contributing factor for the projected overspend as a high number of providers have challenged the uplift awarded for care package costs. Income from Health Partners is an ongoing challenge, with the figures for the previous financial year (2025/26) only recently confirmed. There is a pressure of just under £0.3m as the budgeted amounts are higher than will actually be received according to the latest forecasts.

Dependency on partner organisations (housing associations) creates recovery risk if delivery partners do not resolve contractor issues.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring 2026_27 as at Month 4
findings.headline: Schools DSG forecast overspend of £18.18m with cumulative deficit rising to £38.72m, addressed by new High Needs Stability Grant but future funding uncertain
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £235.61m spend on DSG services against £219.23m funding, an in-year underfunding of £18.18m. The High Needs Block is overspending by £18.42m, driven by rising demand (2,236 EHCPs at end June 2026, up 8% year-on-year) against frozen government funding. The cumulative deficit is projected at £38.72m by year-end. The DfE has introduced a new High Needs Stability Grant expected to write off 90% of the prior-year deficit (£20.52m at March 2026), subject to SEND Reform Plan approval (expected September 2026). However, the DfE has made clear that future support 'will not be unlimited' and there is 'not yet clarity' on support levels for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits.
findings.matters: A £38.72m potential deficit represents a major contingent liability. Although the new grant will write off most of the prior-year deficit, uncertainty about future years' support (described as not unlimited and contingent on delivering transformation) creates medium-term budget risk. The structural driver—rising EHCP demand against frozen funding—is unresolved.
findings.figures: £18.18m in-year overspend; £38.72m cumulative deficit before grant; 2,236 EHCPs (8% increase year-on-year); High Needs Block overspend £18.42m; government funding frozen at 2025/26 levels
findings.quote: The council is projected to spend £235.61m, including £1.805m future demand, on DSG funded education services in 2026/27 compared to a grant allocation of £219.23m (including recoupment). This represents an in-year underfunding of £18.18m. There is not yet clarity about whether the DfE will provide similar levels of support for deficits that may accumulate in 2026/27 and 2027/28. They have confirmed that they will take 'an appropriate and proportionate approach' but that it will not be 'unlimited'.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring 2026_27 as at Month 4
findings.headline: Savings target only 68% delivered in-year (£2.34m of £3.43m), with £0.28m marked Red and just £0.22m mitigations identified against £0.50m shortfall
findings.detail: The council budgeted £3.43m savings for 2026/27. At Month 4, £2.34m (68%) is forecast to be delivered in-year and £0.87m (25%) delayed to future years, totalling 93% expected delivery. However, £0.28m (8%) is marked Red with no path to delivery. The council has identified £0.22m mitigations to offset the shortfall but reports that 'Further mitigation measures will be sought', indicating a £0.06m gap that remains unresolved. Key unachievable items include £0.05m Promoting Independence savings in Adult Social Care and £0.05m+ in events and contract rationalisation income.
findings.matters: Budget plans depend on delivering planned savings. Where only 68% is achieved in-year and 7% cannot be delivered at all, this raises questions about the realism of the financial plan and the council's ability to execute savings. Reliance on future mitigation measures rather than identified actions suggests financial flexibility is being eroded.
findings.figures: £3.43m total savings target; £2.34m (68%) in-year delivery; £0.87m (25%) delayed; £0.28m (8%) Red; £0.22m mitigations identified
findings.quote: £2.34m (68%) of agreed savings are forecast to be delivered in 2026/27 with a further £0.87m (25%) of savings which are expected to be delivered but will be delayed giving overall savings expected to be achieved of £3.19m (93%). £0.22m of savings mitigations have been identified to offset the delayed and non-deliverable savings. Further mitigation measures will be sought.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring 2026_27 as at Month 4
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation driving £2.14m Place Directorate overspend, with demand significantly exceeding forecast despite council efforts to reduce volume
findings.detail: The main driver of the General Fund overspend is Community Housing, which is £2.34m adverse. Within this, Accommodation Services is £1.92m overspent due to higher-than-forecast demand for temporary housing, compounded by increased demand for larger and higher-cost properties. The council has reduced households in temporary accommodation from over 1,000 to under 875 over the past 12 months, but the costs of accommodating remaining households continue to rise. Private Leasing Scheme voids have reduced to c.75 but still create cost pressures.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a structural demand pressure that the council cannot easily control. Rising costs despite falling volumes suggest the pool of households requiring accommodation is becoming more complex and expensive to house, creating an unsustainable spending trajectory unless housing supply increases or demand shifts.
findings.figures: £2.34m Community Housing overspend; £1.92m Accommodation Service adverse variance; households reduced from 1,000+ to <875; c.75 void properties in PLS

findings.headline: Both pension administration performance indicators are in red status, with 45.3% of total cases overdue against a 10% target and 31.7% of cases overdue by 31+ days against a 10% target.
findings.detail: Outstanding processes have risen to 738, with 106 cases overdue by 31+ days. The causes are identified: year-end return processing (326 leaver cases), an eight-week suspension of transfer processing following a SCAPE rate change (256 outstanding transfers), digital payslips implementation, and short-term staff sickness requiring resource reallocation. The council states this is temporary pressure and that the historic backlog remains cleared.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand whether pension administration performance issues indicate broader operational weakness or are genuinely temporary. Red status and significant deviation from target represents substantial operational degradation requiring management response.
findings.figures: 45.3% total cases overdue (target ≤10%), 31.7% cases overdue by 31+ days (target ≤10%), 738 outstanding processes, 106 cases overdue by 31+ days
findings.quote: 45.3%  -  Outside  of  target  and  above  backlog  threshold

findings.paper_title: 6b. Annex B - Pension Administration Projects Update_ Pension Fund Panel _ 20260923
findings.headline: Three amber-rated project risks—historical data gaps, beneficiary tracing failures, and system delays—each carry potential for regulatory penalties if they prevent statutory compliance.
findings.detail: The project carries three amber risks (all scored 12/12): missing employer records from 2005 onwards, inability to locate beneficiaries for death grant payments, and Civica software delays. The risk register explicitly notes that each could result in 'financial penalties if regulatory bodies impose them for non-compliance'. The project must recalculate survivor pensions and death grants back up to 20 years and complete all payments by 1 January 2028.
findings.matters: A pension fund facing multiple amber risks to regulatory compliance creates uncertainty about whether the council will incur unexpected costs and penalties. Lenders assess councils' ability to meet legal obligations.
findings.figures: Three risks scored 12/12; retrospective payments required back to December 2005; statutory deadline 1 January 2028
findings.quote: Financial penalties if regulatory bodies impose them for non-compliance

findings.paper_title: 6b. Annex B - Pension Administration Projects Update_ Pension Fund Panel _ 20260923
findings.headline: Critical external dependency on Civica software provider for pension rectification system remains unscheduled as of September 2026.
findings.detail: The project plan identifies as amber risk (score 12/12) that the bulk rectification software needed to recalculate survivor pensions and death grants has no confirmed delivery dates from Civica. The plan simply states dates are 'to be confirmed'. This software is on the critical path: without it, benefit recalculations cannot be processed. Non-delivery or delay could prevent the council meeting the 1 January 2028 statutory deadline.
findings.matters: An unconfirmed external dependency in a regulatory project with fixed deadline signals governance risk. Vendor delays could force the council to miss statutory compliance deadline and face financial penalties.
findings.figures: Amber risk rating 12/12 (likelihood 4, impact 3); Statutory deadline 1 January 2028
findings.quote: Work with the software provider to implement and test the bulk rectification software for benefit recalculations. Dates to be confirmed with the administration software provider (Civica).

findings.paper_title: 7a. Annex A - Governance and Risk Update_ Pension Fund Panel _ 20260923
findings.headline: Pension fund administration transitioning from legislative uncertainty to implementation of "Fit for the Future" reform programme
findings.detail: Following publication of final statutory guidance at end of June 2026, the risk has moved from legislative uncertainty about the major "Fit for the Future" pension reforms to the delivery and implementation phase. The risk remains Amber-rated during this execution period.
findings.matters: Large-scale regulatory implementation projects create operational, compliance, and cost risks; lenders track whether councils have capacity to deliver major reforms without disrupting core services.

findings.headline: McCloud Annual Benefit Statements breach report filed with Pensions Regulator due to software delivery delays past 31 August statutory deadline

findings.paper_title: Housing Management System (HMS)_ Additional Funding Request
findings.headline: Phase 3 promised 'substantial decrease in contact centre demand' and 'cashable efficiencies' are unquantified and unproven
findings.detail: Phase 3 is presented as delivering 'a substantial decrease in contact centre demand' and 'the realisation of cashable efficiencies across the council'. However, the paper does not quantify the scale or timing of these savings. Phases 1 and 2 only recently went live (Phase 1 December 2025, Phase 2 still rolling out Spring/Summer 2026), so there is no evidence yet that completed phases are delivering measurable operational gains or cost reductions.
findings.matters: The council is committing additional HRA borrowing partly on the basis of future operational efficiencies that are neither quantified nor yet validated by completed phases. If Phase 3 savings do not materialise, the council carries debt burden without offsetting benefits. This is a key risk for assessing financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Phase 3 promises 'substantial decrease in contact centre demand' and 'cashable efficiencies'—amounts and timescales not specified
findings.quote: Phase 3 (Engage Modules) will introduce digitally enabled, resident self-service giving tenants the capacity to review, amend and update their housing account. As well as being a vast improvement for tenants, this change is expected to result in a substantial decrease in contact centre demand and an enhancement in data accuracy.

findings.paper_title: Housing Management System (HMS)_ Additional Funding Request
findings.headline: Implementation team is contractor-dependent with contract expiry risk and potential 6-month restart delay
findings.detail: The Digital Implementation Team critical to delivery is 'largely composed of contractors'. If the team departs before project completion, 'skills and knowledge will be lost' and 'a restart of the project may require up to 6 months to onboard new resources'. The NEC contract expires 31 July 2026, while Phases 3 and 4 are targeted for October 2026—only a 3-month completion window after contract end. This creates execution risk and potential for stranded investment.
findings.matters: A £4.6m capital investment critically dependent on contractor continuity faces execution risk. Loss of momentum could force a 6-month restart, adding cost or potentially stranding the prior £4.2m investment if the project cannot recover. This is a key dependency for lenders assessing project viability.
findings.figures: Contract expires 31 July 2026; Phases 3&4 due October 2026 (3-month window); 6-month potential restart delay if paused
findings.quote: There is a risk that should the Implementation Team depart prematurely before all planned modules can fully be implemented, skills and knowledge will be lost as the team is largely composed of contractors. A pause in the project implementation will mean contractors will be released and a restart of the project may require up to 6 months to onboard new resources to restart the project.

findings.paper_title: Housing Management System (HMS)_ Additional Funding Request
findings.headline: Capital project has grown 76% beyond initial budget, now requiring additional HRA borrowing
findings.detail: The NEC Housing Management System project was budgeted at £2.615m when approved in November 2023. Following scope expansion for data cleansing and system integration, combined with implementation delays, the council approved £4.220m. This request adds a further £372,088, bringing the total to £4.592m. The council attributes the growth to 'additional work required to cleanse and rationalise its data' and notes 'the programme has also incurred delays as a result of the completion of this additional work'.
findings.matters: A 76% cost overrun on a capital project, funded through incremental HRA borrowing approvals (November 2023, September 2025, delegated authority, and now June 2026), signals either poor initial scoping or significant scope creep. For a lender assessing the council's financial position, this adds to debt burden without yet-proven benefits from earlier phases.
findings.figures: Initial budget (Nov 2023): £2.615m; Current approved: £4.220m; Additional requested: £372,088; Total projected: £4.592m (76% growth)
findings.quote: Accordingly the Council has revisited the budget for the NEC implementation programme with an additional £1.160m approved by the Corporate & Resources committee in September 2025. A further budget of £445k was subsequently approved under delegated authority bringing the total current budget for the NEC Housing Management System project at £4,219,761.

findings.paper_title: Soft FM Contract Award
findings.headline: Soft FM costs consistently exceed the dedicated annual budget allocation of £1.10m and are absorbed through reallocation within the wider Property and Projects budget.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that anticipated service costs are higher than the annual FM budget of £1.10m, creating a budget pressure. However, the council notes that these costs have historically been contained within the wider Property and Projects Service budgets through betterment in areas such as commercial rental income. The new contract value is £7.51m excluding VAT over five years, broadly in line with historic spend. The council assumes this ongoing cost can continue to be managed within existing resources.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council is managing a structural gap between dedicated FM budgets and actual costs through cross-service reallocation, which depends on achieving betterment in other service areas like commercial property income.
findings.figures: Dedicated FM budget: £1.10m annually; New contract value: £7.51m excluding VAT over five years; Contract term: 3 years with optional 2-year extension
findings.quote: It is noted that the anticipated cost of the services is higher than the annual budget of £1.10m which presents a pressure to the Council's FM budget. However, the total cost of the new contract is broadly in line with the historic cost of the services which has been contained within the wider Property and Projects Service budgets.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Placement costs for children in care rising 8.4% above inflation, driven by complexity and market shortages
findings.detail: Children Looked After services overspent by £1.03m. The shift in case mix is material: fewer children in lower-cost in-house foster care (39 budgeted vs 35 actual) and more in expensive independent fostering agencies (28 budgeted vs 34 actual) and children's homes, due to placement complexity. Average placement costs rose 8.4% against an inflationary rise included in the budget. Children's cases also show increased complexity requiring higher-cost support. This is part of a wider pattern: ASC operations overspent £0.83m partly due to complexity and market pressures in adult care.
findings.matters: Rising placement costs outpacing inflation and budget assumptions is a leading indicator of social care market stress. It suggests either the council underestimated complexity or the care market is becoming more expensive. Both are concerning for councils' medium-term spending.
findings.figures: Children Looked After overspend £1.03m; placement cost inflation 8.4% vs budgeted inflation; 34 independent fostering placements vs 28 budgeted; 25 residential placements; ASC Operations overspend £0.83m
findings.quote: The average cost of placements has also exceeded the inflationary rise included in the budget for all placement types - seeing an increase on average of 8.40%.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme £36.17m underspend (20% of budget) with £35.66m rephased into 2026/27, signalling delivery delays across the portfolio
findings.detail: Against a capital budget of £184.21m, the council spent £148.04m, leaving a £36.17m underspend. While £35.66m is being rephased into next year, this indicates systematic delays. The Place directorate alone has £14.68m underspend, mainly due to Cambridge Road Estate (£14.99m HRA underspend) where Phase 1a faced delays in commissioning the district heat network and securing Building Safety Regulator approval—handover occurred in April 2026, not by 31 March. General Fund Property projects £4.24m underspent due to delayed commencements and contractor reprofiling.
findings.matters: Large slippages suggest the council struggles with project delivery and forecasting. For a lender, this raises questions about the council's ability to execute major capital schemes (housing, infrastructure) on time and budget. It also creates cash flow uncertainty.
findings.figures: £36.17m underspend (20%) on £184.21m budget; £35.66m rephased to 2026/27; General Fund underspend £18.68m; HRA underspend £17.49m; Cambridge Road Estate Phase 1a £14.99m underspend
findings.quote: The 2025-26 Capital programme has recorded an underspend of £36.17m...Within the underspend an amount of £35.66m is being requested to be rephased into 2026/27 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspend of £2.96m, drawing down reserves to zero transfer position
findings.detail: The HRA budgeted for a £2.43m contribution to reserves but actual outturn was an overspend of £2.96m, requiring a drawdown from reserves of £0.53m. This reversed what was forecast at month 9 (a £1.07m positive transfer to reserves). Multiple pressures drove this: electrical repairs (£0.50m extra) for mandatory smoke detector replacements; damp and mould work driven by Awaab's Law (£0.10m); bad debt provisions increased £0.16m; and interest charge variance of £0.83m. The HRA fund balance fell to £15.19m.
findings.matters: The HRA is self-financing and relies on reserves to weather demand shocks. Drawing down reserves rather than building them indicates the housing service is operationally under stress. Multiple £0.1-0.5m pressures suggest the budget model is not capturing true cost drivers.
findings.figures: £2.96m overspend vs £2.43m budgeted contribution; £0.53m drawn from reserves; HRA fund balance £15.19m (down from £15.72m); electrical repairs £0.50m extra; damp/mould £0.10m; bad debt provision increase £0.16m
findings.quote: The HRA is overspent by £2.96m at year end which results in an outturn deficit position of £0.53m. This will reduce the HRA balance to £15.19m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: 12% of planned savings (£0.80m of £6.66m) will not be delivered, requiring reactive mitigations
findings.detail: The council planned £6.66m of savings for 2025/26. By year-end, £0.80m (12%) were rated RED as undeliverable, £1.30m (19.5%) were AMBER/delayed, and only £4.56m (68.5%) were GREEN/delivered. The failures include Children's Services savings on kinship care (£0.20m) and staffing reviews (£0.16m) where implementation proved more complex than assumed; a Place Directorate saving on Ancient Marketplace income (£0.10m) that required tenants be given rent-free periods; and a cross-council leadership restructuring that did not fully materialise. To cover these, the council identified £1.49m in reactive mitigations.
findings.matters: A lender depends on councils' ability to execute savings plans. When 12% fail and 19.5% slip, it signals forecast risk. The reliance on finding £1.49m in reactive mitigations to cover unplanned shortfalls suggests budget planning and control challenges.
findings.figures: £6.66m planned; £0.80m (12%) Red-rated non-delivery; £1.30m (19.5%) Amber-rated delays; £4.56m (68.5%) Green-rated delivery; £1.49m reactive mitigations required
findings.quote: Savings totalling £6.66m were included in the 2025/26 approved budget. The final position is of the £6.66m planned savings, £4.56m (68.5%) were Green (delivered in full), £1.30m (19.5%) were given an overall rating of Amber (delayed) and £0.80m (12.0%) were rated Red (will not be delivered).

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation overspend of £6.23m driven by homelessness demand 4x higher than historical norms, with no resolution in sight
findings.detail: The council is now receiving 130 homelessness approaches per month, up from a historic average of 30. This has driven a £6.23m overspend in Community Housing despite efforts to reduce the temporary accommodation population. The council has increased rates and incentives to secure nightly-paid accommodation and private sector leases, and is paying void costs on empty properties. Delays in the council's own mitigation programmes (acquisitions, new supply) mean the demand surge is not being offset.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a demand-led statutory duty that cannot be refused. A 4x surge in demand that costs £6.23m overspend in a single year indicates the council's housing strategy is not keeping pace with housing crisis trends. This is creating recurring, growing expenditure.
findings.figures: 130 homelessness approaches/month vs 30 historic average; £6.23m overspend; c.930 households in TA (down 100 from peak but still very high); Nightly Paid Accommodation costs worse than forecast; PSL void costs including rents and council tax
findings.quote: The council is experiencing a rapid and sustained increase in homelessness approaches from residents to whom it owes a statutory duty of care, and who have been unable to afford or secure housing in the borough...averaging at 130 approaches a month compared to a historic average of 30.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will reach £38.63m by March 2027 unless government intervention materialises
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £12.75m in 2025/26, growing the DSG deficit from £12.40m to £20.54m. Projections show this rising to £38.63m in 2026/27. The council is depending on government delivery of a 'High Needs Stability Grant' in autumn 2026 that would cover 90% of deficits, but this is subject to approval of a SEND Reform Plan that is still being drafted. The deficit remains legally ringfenced outside the General Fund only until March 2028.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a £20m structural deficit in schools funding is temporary or permanent, and whether government pledges carry delivery risk. The deficit trajectory is material to the council's medium-term solvency.
findings.figures: £20.54m deficit at 31 March 2026 (up from £12.40m); forecast to rise £18.01m in 2026/27 to £38.63m; 2,169 EHCPs (184 net new in year); High Needs Block overspend £12.75m
findings.quote: The accumulated deficit on the ringfenced Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) Reserve is £20.54m at 31st March 2025...is forecast to rise by £18.01m during 2026/27 due to the overspend on the High Needs Block.

findings.headline: HRA property acquisitions overrunning budget by £3m, driven by purchase of properties using Right to Buy receipts

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council adopted a strategy of short-term and internal borrowing to avoid locking in long-term debt at rates above 5%.
findings.detail: The council deliberately minimized long-term borrowing above 5% and instead relied on short-term loans and internal resources. During 2025/26, the council raised two short-term loans (£25m at 4.05%, £32.42m at 3.89%) and refinanced maturing debt into shorter tranches. This strategy is prudent if rates fall but creates refinancing risk if rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: Short-term strategies work only if rates subsequently fall; sustained high rates create rollover risk and could force acceptance of unfavorable refinancing terms.
findings.figures: £25m at 4.05% (Nov 2025); £32.42m at 3.89% (Feb 2026); £50m debt refinanced into two £25m tranches at 4.07% and 4.18%
findings.quote: the council has sought to minimise the taking on of long-term borrowing at elevated levels (over 5%) and has focused on a policy of internal and temporary borrowing, supplemented by short-dated borrowing (under 5 years) as appropriate.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Public Works Loan Board borrowing costs rose sharply: 10-year fixed rates increased from 5.38% to 5.72%, with highs of 5.88%.
findings.detail: The PWLB certainty rate for 10-year loans rose 34 basis points over the financial year. During the year, rates reached as high as 5.88% for 10-year borrowing, 6.37% for 20-year, and 6.24% for 50-year loans. These elevated rates directly increase the cost of the £166m planned future borrowing through the PWLB.
findings.matters: PWLB rates set the cost of future council borrowing; sustained rates above 5.5% materially increase debt service costs and may constrain capital plans.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB certainty rate: 5.38% to 5.72% (34 basis points); high of 5.88%; 20-year rates 5.71%-6.37%; 50-year rates 5.46%-6.24%
findings.quote: The PWLB certainty rate for 10-year maturity loans was 5.38% at the beginning of the period and 5.72% at the end. The lowest available 10-year maturity certainty rate was 5.13% and the highest was 5.88%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: A £5m LOBO loan faced a 203 basis point rate increase, forcing the council to repay using cash reserves rather than refinance at the higher rate.
findings.detail: One LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loan saw the lender exercise the right to increase the interest rate from 4.25% to 6.28% on a loan maturing in December 2054. The council repaid the full £5m on 17 December 2025 using cash resources rather than accept the new rate. This shows the council faces material rate shock risk on refinanced debt.
findings.matters: LOBO calls demonstrate council exposure to unilateral rate increases; the decision to repay using cash signals the council views such increases as unaffordable, constraining future refinancing flexibility.
findings.figures: £5m LOBO loan; rate increase from 4.25% to 6.28% (203 basis points); repaid 17 December 2025
findings.quote: The increase proposed was from 4.25% to 6.28% and the £5m loan had a maturity date of December 2054. The council elected to repay the £5m LOBO loan in full on 17th December 2025 at no additional cost using cash resources.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: External debt grew 15.8% year-on-year to £379m, with plans to borrow a further £166m toward the £545m capital requirement.
findings.detail: Council's external debt increased from £327.39m (31 March 2025) to £379.03m (31 March 2026), an increase of £51.64m. With a Capital Financing Requirement of £545.07m, the under-borrowed position of £154.37m indicates the council plans to borrow approximately £166m more over future years to complete capital spending.
findings.matters: Lenders track council debt trajectory relative to revenue; rapid growth combined with planned further borrowing affects medium-term leverage and debt sustainability.
findings.figures: External debt £379.03m (31 March 2026), up £51.64m (15.8%) from prior year; CFR £545.07m; planned additional borrowing £166m
findings.quote: The Council's overall external debt at 31 March 2026 totalled £379.03m, of which £318.41m was with the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB), £34m was with individual banks, and £26.63m was an interest-free loan from the Greater London Authority.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit report
findings.headline: Planning enforcement backlog and weak performance oversight being addressed through additional staffing but key control framework elements not yet embedded
findings.detail: Development Management audit (Reasonable Assurance) found significant backlog of enforcement complaints and cases remaining open for extended periods, underdeveloped performance monitoring with limited reporting on caseloads. This is the only Priority 1 recommendation from 2025/26 that remains outstanding. While significant progress made and backlog substantially reduced through additional staffing, the Enforcement Manager post remains vacant and formal performance targets and reporting arrangements not yet implemented.
findings.matters: Persistent resourcing pressures in enforcement create risk that improvements are not sustained. Overdue recommendation indicates management is struggling to close a known control gap.
findings.figures: 1 Priority 1 recommendation outstanding/overdue from 2025/26; backlog substantially reduced but not fully resolved
findings.quote: Significant progress has been made, including a full review of cases, a substantial reduction in backlog, and improved caseload management following additional staffing. However, key elements of the control framework are not yet fully embedded, with the Enforcement Manager post still vacant and formal performance targets and reporting arrangements yet to be implemented.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit report
findings.headline: Net Zero 2030 commitment lacks fully costed implementation plan with no clear funding view, creating delivery and financial risk
findings.detail: Climate Change audit (Reasonable Assurance overall) identified Priority 1 finding: while a strategy has been developed, costs of delivery, funding requirements, and prioritization of interventions have not been clearly defined or aligned to available resources. This creates significant delivery and financial risk with no clear affordability view.
findings.matters: A major strategic commitment without costed implementation plan means the council cannot assess financial impact or viability. This indicates risk that the 2030 target is unachievable within available resources.
findings.figures: 1 Priority 1 finding; 2030 Net Zero target
findings.quote: The Priority 1 finding relates to the absence of a fully costed implementation plan to support delivery of the Council's Net Zero target by 2030. While a strategy has been developed, costs of delivery, funding requirements, and the prioritisation of interventions have not been clearly defined or aligned to available resources.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit report
findings.headline: Housing voids: no cost recovery recharges processed since 2022/23 despite established policy, creating avoidable financial loss
findings.detail: Voids audit (Limited Assurance) found no recharges have been processed since 2022/23 despite policy requiring recovery of costs attributable to tenant damage. This represents departure from previous practice where recharge income was generated annually. Additionally, financial monitoring of voids is incomplete with gaps in in-year reporting and no accounting for void rental loss at time of audit.
findings.matters: Failure to enforce a legitimate cost recovery policy represents avoidable income loss to the housing revenue account. Weak financial reporting on voids means the council lacks visibility of the actual cost of vacancies.
findings.figures: No recharges since 2022/23; 2 Priority 1 findings
findings.quote: Audit identified that no recharges have been processed since 2022/23, despite an established policy requiring the recovery of costs attributable to tenant damage. This departs from previous practice, where recharge income was generated annually, and reflects gaps in operational processes, clarity of responsibilities, and resourcing.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit report
findings.headline: Domiciliary Care contract monitoring framework not being delivered consistently with gaps due to resourcing constraints
findings.detail: Domiciliary Care audit (Limited Assurance) found monitoring not delivered consistently with missing/incomplete records, scheduled meetings not undertaken due to resourcing pressures, and issues identified but not systematically recorded or followed through. This weakens assurance that provider risks are being effectively identified and managed.
findings.matters: Weak contract monitoring of domiciliary care providers creates risk of service failure, safeguarding incidents, and financial loss affecting vulnerable service users.
findings.figures: 1 Priority 1 finding; Limited Assurance opinion
findings.quote: Audit identified that contract monitoring is not being delivered consistently in line with the established framework. Testing found gaps in monitoring activity, including missing or incomplete records and evidence that scheduled meetings were not undertaken due to resourcing constraints.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit report
findings.headline: Inadequate segregation of duties in Cash & Bank with key officers holding unrestricted system access across financial platforms during staffing shortages
findings.detail: The Cash & Bank audit (Limited Assurance) found insufficient separation between system administration and operational responsibilities. Key officers held administrative access across Business World, PT-X, Pay360 and banking platforms while also undertaking transactional activities. PT-X system also showed lack of independent administration, excessive access, inconsistent role definitions, and unverified user credentials.
findings.matters: Weak segregation of duties is a fundamental internal control failure that increases fraud and error risk in cash and bank transactions. This directly undermines financial control and audit trail integrity.
findings.figures: 2 Priority 1 findings (both implemented); Limited Assurance opinion on financial system
findings.quote: Audit identified that, during periods of reduced staffing, there was insufficient separation between system administration and transactional responsibilities within the Financial Control Team. In particular, key officers held administrative access across multiple financial systems (including Business World, PT-X, Pay360 and banking platforms) while also undertaking operational activities, limiting independent oversight.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit report
findings.headline: Fire safety compliance failures in Housing for Older People with delayed remedial action implementation
findings.detail: The audit of Housing for Older People identified 4 Priority 1 findings covering fire risk assessment tracking weaknesses, incomplete remedial actions (4 of 9 high-risk actions not completed at audit), outdated policies not aligned to Fire Safety (Residential Evacuation Plans) (England) Regulations 2025, and privacy consent arrangements not aligned to regulatory requirements. The council received Limited Assurance overall.
findings.matters: These are material compliance failures in a regulated service for vulnerable residents. Incomplete fire safety actions pose direct safety risk and expose the council to legal and regulatory liability.
findings.figures: 4 out of 9 high-risk fire remedial actions not completed; 4 Priority 1 findings
findings.quote: Audit testing identified delays in completing fire risk assessment (FRA) remedial actions within required timeframes. Of nine high-risk actions reviewed, four had not been completed at the time of audit, and further testing identified delays in implementing medium-priority actions, including safety-critical measures such as fire doors, alarm systems, and fire safety instructions.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Pension Fund Accounts Audit Findings
findings.paper_url: https://kingston.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s113632/10. 2024_25 Pension Fund Accounts Audit Outcomes Report.pdf
findings.headline: Kingston's pension fund controls lack system-enforced authorization for journal entries; gap remains until 2026/27 upgrade
findings.detail: A control deficiency identified in the 2023/24 audit—the absence of a formal two-step, system-based authorization process for journal approvals—has been mitigated by introduction of a manual approval process in 2024/25. The audit found no unauthorized or inappropriate journal entries under this manual regime. However, the permanent solution (system-enforced control via Business World upgrade) is not scheduled until 2026/27, leaving a control gap in the interim.
findings.matters: A lender assesses operational control quality and internal audit findings; control weaknesses in pension fund accounting, even if currently mitigated, indicate governance gaps that could materially affect financial reporting integrity.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: The audit report notes the current lack of a formal two step, system based authorisation process for journal approvals. This risk was initially identified during the 2023/24 audit. Officers responded by introducing a manual journal approval process in 2024/25, which has mitigated the risk.

findings.paper_title: Annex 01 - Risk Assumptions 26_27 , item 6.
findings.headline: Council targets £3.43M in savings for 2026/27; a 3-month delivery delay would result in £0.86M budget shortfall needing to be covered from General Fund Balance
findings.detail: Rated 3/3 inherent and 2/2 residual risk. Savings are reviewed by SLT and WLT for achievability; progress monitored monthly. Non-achievement would need to be covered from General Fund Balance (£19.6M total).
findings.matters: Savings are a key component of a balanced budget. Slippage is material and would directly reduce the council's buffer.
findings.figures: £3.43M total savings assumed; 3-month delay = £0.86M shortfall
findings.quote: Delivery of all of the agreed savings and future savings targets is not achieved

findings.paper_title: Annex 01 - Risk Assumptions 26_27 , item 6.
findings.headline: Removal of DSG deficit override in March 2028 could leave council with up to £22M liability if government provides no additional funding
findings.detail: The government has not yet confirmed how it will manage accrued High Needs Block deficits when the override ends. RBK has an accrued deficit at 31/3/2026 of ~£21M (90% covered by grant, 10% = ~£2.1M retained) plus forecasts a further £20M deficit. Total potential liability ~£22.1M; assuming 50% retained = £11.05M impact on General Fund Balance.
findings.matters: This is a material contingent liability that could force exceptional financial support if the government does not fund it. The uncertainty and magnitude are both concerning.
findings.figures: ~£21M accrued deficit, ~£20M further deficit forecast, total ~£22.1M, 50% assumption = £11.05M
findings.quote: Government have announced, linked to SEND Reform that Local Authorities will not be expected to meet DSG deficits after the end of the Statutory Override in March 2028. Details have not yet been provided on how this change will be managed or implemented.

findings.paper_title: Annex 01 - Risk Assumptions 26_27 , item 6.
findings.headline: Council forecasts a structural budget gap growing from £10M in 2027/28 to £24M by 2029/30 with no confirmed plan to close it
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges it does not have a robust plan to close this gap. Mitigation relies on transformation funding and an assumption that 50% of future gaps will be met from additional savings or drawdown from the Economic Risk Reserve or General Fund Balance. This is rated 3/4 residual risk (medium probability, major impact).
findings.matters: A £24M structural deficit is unsustainable and signals that deep service cuts or significant additional funding will be needed within three years. Lenders need to know whether the council can resolve this without exceptional support.
findings.figures: £10M gap in 2027/28, increasing to £24.06M by 2029/30
findings.quote: With a £10M budget gap in 2027/28 increasing to £24.06M by 2029/30 a robust plan for achieving financial sustainability needs to be established.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: Adult Social Care facing £1m new ongoing pressure from National Insurance uplifts effective April 2025
findings.detail: Uplifts to National Insurance employer contributions came into effect April 2025 and created a £1m ongoing pressure on Adult Social Care provider costs. Combined with rising demand and complexity in Mental Health and Physical Support services, this creates a permanent structural cost increase.
findings.matters: This is a permanent new cost driver that will recur annually, reducing financial flexibility and adding to the unachievable budget gap.
findings.figures: £1m new ongoing pressure on Adult Social Care from National Insurance; identified as growth item in 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: Uplifts to National Insurance employer contributions (alongside inflation and increases in London Living wage) came into effect in April 2025 and had a significant impact on Adult Social Care provider costs, this has created an ongoing pressure of £1m.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: HRA £105m capital programme contingent on government rent convergence decision not yet made
findings.detail: The council's 30-year Housing Revenue Account business plan assumes a return to stable rent convergence formula. Any continued cap on social rents without subsidy will impair the ability to fund the £105.07m HRA capital programme and Cambridge Road Estate regeneration over 2026-2030.
findings.matters: A £105m capital programme is a major commitment. If government does not allow rents to converge, the council may face difficult choices to reduce this programme or fund it from general reserves.
findings.figures: £105.07m HRA capital programme 2026/27-2029/30; £248m total capital programme (general fund £142.93m + HRA £105.07m)
findings.quote: Any continued "cap" on social rents without corresponding subsidy will impair our ability to fund the £105.07m HRA capital program and the Cambridge Road Estate regeneration.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: S151 Officer warns reserves will be 'significantly challenged' and must be kept under 'close review'
findings.detail: The S151 officer states that the level of available reserves will be 'significantly challenged over the period of the MTFS' and that the level of potential financial risk identified would 'far exceed' the risk reserves available should all risks materialise in one year. Reserves must be kept at minimum to weather future shocks.
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer against unforeseen events. If reserves are already significantly challenged by identified risks, the council has little resilience to absorb unexpected costs.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £19.63m; identified risks in Annex 1 exceed available reserves; earmarked reserves £49.96m
findings.quote: It should, however, be recognised that the level of potential financial risk identified in Annex 1 would far exceed the level of risk reserves available should all of these present in year.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: Children's Social Care experiencing ten-fold increase in complex cases compared to 2018/19
findings.detail: Children's services are facing a tenfold increase in complex case numbers compared to 2018/19, alongside rising complexity of needs. This creates exponential cost pressure on a statutory service the council must fund.
findings.matters: Complex cases are significantly more expensive to manage, and a tenfold increase suggests either a genuine demographic/social shift or identification of unmet need that now requires expensive intervention.
findings.figures: Ten-fold increase in complex cases compared to 2018/19
findings.quote: Children's Social Care are seeing a ten fold increase in complex cases compared to 2018/19.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation crisis creating £5.62m annual overspend with structural drivers
findings.detail: Homelessness approaches are higher than anticipated, private sector landlord properties are being lost faster than forecast, and mitigation measures are delayed. The council is increasingly reliant on expensive Nightly Paid Accommodation rather than council-owned stock. This structural mismatch is forecast to cost £5.62m in 2025/26 and is identified as a continuing demand pressure.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a statutory service that councils cannot refuse to provide, making this a non-discretionary cost growing faster than funding, creating permanent budget pressure.
findings.figures: £5.62m Community Housing overspend in 2025/26; higher than anticipated homelessness approaches; faster than forecast loss of Private Sector Leasing properties; identified as acute ongoing demand
findings.quote: The Council has seen a higher than anticipated number of homelessness approaches, greater than forecast losses of Private Sector Leasing properties and longer lead in times to deliver some of the anticipated mitigating actions. This has resulted in a greater reliance on the use of more expensive Nightly Paid Accommodation (NPA).

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: Cumulative MTFS deficit of £24.06m by 2029/30 with no credible savings plan to bridge it
findings.detail: The council projects deficits of £9.99m (2027/28), £6.60m (2028/29), and £7.47m (2029/30), totalling £24.06m across the medium term. Total savings identified across the entire MTFS period are only £3.43m in 2026/27. The S151 officer acknowledges 'further service efficiencies and income generation will be needed... to ensure there is a sustainable way to deliver balanced budgets'.
findings.matters: A £24m structural deficit over four years with no identified savings programme suggests the council will be unable to achieve a balanced budget without service closures, significant tax rises, or government bailout.
findings.quote: At £10.00m, the level of savings needed to balance the budget for 2027/28, increasing to £24.06m by 2029/30, will present a significant challenge to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget 'balanced' entirely through one-off funding and reserve draws that reverse in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council has achieved a balanced 2026/27 budget by suspending contributions to borrowing reserves, removing the DSG deficit contribution, and using collection fund surpluses. These one-off measures total over £10m. When these reverse in 2027/28, the council faces a £9.99m deficit immediately, rising to £24.06m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: One-off accounting measures used to balance budgets are a warning sign of structural unaffordability and unsustainable practice.
findings.figures: £1.137m secondary pension contribution reduction; £2.4m removal of DSG deficit contribution; £2.939m combined other one-offs; 2027/28 budget gap jumps to £10.00m
findings.quote: Whilst it has not been necessary to use reserves directly to meet the budget gap in order to propose a balanced budget for 2026/27 there remains a significant element of one off funding that is being utilised to fund ongoing expenditure... This contributes to the increase in the budget gap for 2027/28 when this funding is removed again.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: 2025/26 current year overspend of £6.15m with no guaranteed mitigation
findings.detail: The council is already £6.15m overspent at month 9 of the current financial year (2025/26), driven primarily by £5.62m overspend on temporary accommodation and homelessness. If this overspend cannot be mitigated in-year, it will need to be met from reserves.
findings.matters: Current year overspends reduce available reserves and foreshadow future years' pressures, increasing risk of reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £6.15m overspend at month 9; Community Housing £5.62m overspend; Adult Social Care £1m new pressure from National Insurance uplifts
findings.quote: At month 9, the Council is reporting a pressure of £6.15m on service spend within Directorates.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: S151 officer warns council risks Section 114 notice if DSG override removed without funding support
findings.detail: The S151 officer's formal statement warns that if the DSG statutory override is removed without substantial additional government support, combined with existing pressures, the council would not be financially sustainable and may need to consider issuing a Section 114 notice.
findings.matters: Section 114 is a formal declaration of financial crisis that triggers government intervention and indicates serious credit risk.
findings.figures: Override expires 1 April 2028; government has committed to 90% support but future tranches unconfirmed
findings.quote: For Kingston, the removal of the override without further substantial financial support, alongside the other financial pressures already identified, would mean that the council would not be financially sustainable over the period of the MTFS without the need for Exceptional Financial Support alongside the possibility of considering the issue of a S114 notice.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026_27- 2029_30 - Budget Council February 2026 , item 6.
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £21m poses existential risk to long-term financial sustainability
findings.detail: Kingston faces a cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of approximately £21m by March 2026, and although the government will fund 90% of the deficit accrued by that date, the council remains liable for 10% of this plus any deficits accrued between 2026 and the removal of the statutory override in March 2028. The S151 officer explicitly identifies this as 'the single greatest threat to Kingston's long term financial sustainability'.
findings.matters: This deficit could force the council into Exceptional Financial Support or a Section 114 notice (formal financial crisis declaration), which affects creditworthiness and lender risk.
findings.figures: £21m cumulative DSG deficit by 31 March 2026; 90% government support confirmed; 10% liability remains; full DSG override removed 1 April 2028
findings.quote: This liability remains the single greatest threat to Kingston's long term financial sustainability.

findings.detail: Children Looked After budget is overspending by £0.907m despite the actual number of children in care falling from 101 to 98. More children are moving from in-house foster care to higher-cost independent fostering agencies and children's homes due to case complexity. Average placement costs have exceeded the inflationary rise in the budget, indicating a structural shift to a higher-cost case mix.
findings.matters: This shows cost control is harder when demand shifts to higher-acuity cases. It's a leading indicator that even with volume reductions, costs can grow—suggesting prior forecasts were optimistic.
findings.figures: £0.907m overspend, 101→98 children looked after, shift to independent agencies
findings.quote: More children are moving from lower cost in-house foster care to higher cost independent fostering agencies and children's home placements due to the complexity of their needs. The average cost of placements has also exceeded the inflationary rise included in the budget for all placement types.

findings.headline: Capital programme showing £9.07m in-year slippage with major projects delayed
findings.detail: The capital programme is £9.07m underspent in-year, with major projects slipping: Kingston Leisure Centre (£3.92m underspend to be rephased), Cambridge Road Estate (£1.55m), and Major Development projects (£4.33m). findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation and homelessness costs spiraling by £5.62m with weakening mitigations
findings.detail: Community Housing (homelessness and TA) is forecasting a £5.62m overspend, an adverse movement of £4.26m from month 6 alone. findings.quote: Costs associated with Homelessness and Temporary Accommodation (TA) are forecast to overspend by £5.62m, an adverse movement of £4.26m from M6. A deep dive of budget forecasting was undertaken during Q3 resulting in a significant increase from M6.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block deficit ballooning from £8.27m to £20.93m in one year
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is overspending by £12.67m at month 9. The accumulated DSG deficit is forecast to grow from £8.27m at 31 March 2025 to £20.93m at 31 March 2026. EHCPs have increased by 145 net to 2,130, with 266 new EHCPs in the first nine months alone. Critically, the statutory override allowing this deficit to sit outside General Fund reserves expires March 2028, at which point the full liability becomes a live budget pressure.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - RBK_ISA260_AGS , item 29.
findings.headline: Lack of formalised agreements on bank accounts held by Council for third parties
findings.detail: The audit identified bank accounts managed by the Council on behalf of third parties without formal agreements defining roles and responsibilities. This creates risk of mismanagement of funds due to lack of clarity. Management acknowledges the recommendation but formalised agreements have not been put in place as of the audit date.
findings.matters: Absence of formal agreements for third-party funds increases risk of disputes, misuse of funds, and unclear accountability for fund management.
findings.figures: Multiple accounts identified, but specific number not stated
findings.quote: We identified a number of bank accounts that are being managed by the Council on behalf of third parties. Upon inquiry with management, we noted the absence of formal agreements with the third parties which creates a risk of mismanagement of the funds due to the lack of clarity of the roles and responsibility of the Council and the third parties in the arrangement.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - RBK_ISA260_AGS , item 29.
findings.headline: Corrected audit misstatements of £8.1m including property valuation errors and demolished asset incorrectly capitalised
findings.detail: Three corrected misstatements totalling £8.1m impact on the deficit were identified and corrected: (1) A demolished asset was transferred into assets under construction and work capitalised, requiring a £15.5m adjustment; (2) A property was valued at the wrong amount in the valuer's report, requiring £3.2m correction; (3) Pension benefits paid were understated by £897k. All were corrected before finalisation but indicate initial control failures over asset accounting.
findings.matters: Material misstatements in draft accounts demonstrate that controls over asset recognition and measurement are not operating effectively, and errors were only caught by audit procedures rather than management controls.
findings.figures: Total corrected misstatements: £8.1m net impact on deficit; component items £15.457m, £3.225m, and £897k
findings.quote: As part of our testing over fixed assets, we noted that the Council had transferred into assets under construction an asset that was demolished, and had begun to capitalise work that had been done in the financial year on the existing land.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - RBK_ISA260_AGS , item 29.
findings.headline: Bank reconciliations incomplete and reconciling items left outstanding for five months
findings.detail: The audit found deficiencies in bank reconciliation procedures: some accounts had no reconciliation prepared, some were not reviewed at all, and reconciling items remained outstanding for extended periods. Specifically, one reconciling item was noted as outstanding for five months. This is a recurring issue from the prior year. The Council states the two main accounts are reconciled daily but has not addressed the systematic deficiency across all accounts.
findings.matters: Weak bank reconciliation controls create risk of undetected fraud, misstatement of cash balances, and loss of funds. Outstanding items for months suggests control procedures are not operating effectively.
findings.figures: Outstanding reconciling items identified; one specifically noted as five months outstanding
findings.quote: The reconciliation statements for some bank accounts were either not reviewed at the end of the month for which they had been prepared or not reviewed at all. A few bank accounts did not have reconciliations prepared. Certain reconciling items remained outstanding for an extended period.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - RBK_ISA260_AGS , item 29.
findings.headline: Property valuations totalling £975m lack formalised review of assumptions, recurring weakness
findings.detail: The audit identified a control deficiency in management's review of property valuations. The Council could not initially produce an engagement letter with the valuer, and the auditor found no formal process to review significant assumptions used by the third-party valuer. This weakness persists despite being flagged previously. Council dwellings (£405m), other land and buildings (£499m), and investment property (£71m) all affected. The auditor notes the control 'does not operate with a level of precision that would allow us to rely on the control'.
findings.matters: Property represents the largest class of assets on the balance sheet; weak controls over valuation assumptions mean material misstatement risk is unmitigated. Auditors described assumptions as 'optimistic but within acceptable range'.
findings.figures: Council dwellings £405m, other land and buildings £499m, investment property £71m; total property valuations £975m
findings.quote: We were unable to obtain an engagement letter between the Council and the valuer and were therefore unable to verify the instructions provided. Secondly, we did not identify a formal process at the Council to review the significant assumptions used by the third party valuer, and noted that this information was not readily available in the final report.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - RBK_ISA260_AGS , item 29.
findings.headline: Journal entry controls allow users to approve their own transactions, recurring from prior year
findings.detail: The Council's ledger system does not enforce segregation of duties in approval of journal entries. Users can post and self-approve journals with no system restriction. This creates a fraud risk and has been flagged as outstanding since the prior year audit. Management acknowledges the issue and plans system upgrades over 12-18 months but has not yet implemented preventative controls.
findings.matters: Lack of segregation of duties is a fundamental internal control weakness that increases fraud risk and reduces the reliability of financial data, directly relevant to lenders assessing governance and financial control strength.
findings.figures: 22 high-risk journals and 36 post-close adjustments examined; control deficiency marked as Priority 1 (fundamental and material)
findings.quote: There is no system-enforced segregation of duties in approving the journals posted by users. We also identified that on some occasions, users approved their own journals as there is no restriction in the system which prevents self-approval. This creates a risk that fraudulent transactions posted and self-approved are undetected.

findings.detail: The original contract covered routine and responsive cleaning. During the contract term, additional services were added that were not in the original scope, deemed necessary to provide a safe environment. These additions contributed to the cost increases.
findings.matters: Unplanned scope additions during a contract indicate inadequate initial needs assessment and weak change control, both concerning to lenders evaluating operational discipline.

findings.matters: Exceeding a contract maximum value indicates weak cost forecasting and procurement planning; the scale of overrun (nearly 50%) raises concerns about financial controls.

findings.paper_title: LATE MATERIAL - Replacement Report - Cloud Data Centre Service Contract Award
findings.headline: AWS invoices in USD; contract is exposed to exchange rate fluctuations with no stated hedging strategy
findings.detail: The paper explicitly identifies that 'the AWS contract is susceptible to exchange rate fluctuations due to invoices being in USD ($) and payments in GBP (£).' No hedging arrangement, forward rate agreement, or currency management approach is mentioned.
findings.matters: On a £7.4M contract over 5 years, sterling depreciation against the dollar creates material cost escalation. A 10% GBP weakness adds roughly £740k to the total cost. Absence of any currency risk mitigation indicates this risk is unmanaged.

findings.paper_title: LATE MATERIAL - Replacement Report - Cloud Data Centre Service Contract Award
findings.headline: Contract is consumption-based with variable costs; £2.0m contingency approved for undefined non-committed expenditure
findings.detail: The contract cost varies with actual monthly usage. The paper approves £2.0m 'in principle' to cover 'currently uncommitted expenditure' and 'transformation opportunities' but does not define what drives these costs. Separately, the service notes it is 'exploring options' to reduce high-consumption software costs like Business World, suggesting known cost control challenges.
findings.matters: Consumption-based pricing on an essential service creates significant budget uncertainty. A £2.0m contingency (roughly £400k per year over 5 years) signals that variable costs are a material concern, yet the paper does not specify what would trigger this expenditure or how it will be controlled.
findings.figures: Committed costs £5.40m; non-committed contingency £2.0m; total £7.40m; annual cost estimate £1.08m (combined with Sutton)

findings.paper_title: LATE MATERIAL - Replacement Report - Cloud Data Centre Service Contract Award
findings.headline: New annual budget cost of £78,000 depends on unconfirmed savings from Guildhall 2 data centre closure
findings.detail: The council states the budgetary pressure 'is expected to be met' from savings when the on-premises Guildhall 2 data centre closes. findings.matters: If the Guildhall 2 closure is delayed or the savings do not materialize, the council has an unafforded £78k annual cost on an essential service. This indicates budget planning based on savings that are not yet confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - RBK - Teckal Company - Member's Agreement JF PA 2023 (7 Oct 25)

This governance structure gives the council tight control but may delay operational decisions.
findings.matters: The control structure ensures the council can enforce strategic direction, but decision-making delays could impact operational agility in a fast-moving housing market. Lenders need clarity on what Reserved Matters apply to borrowing decisions and financial commitments.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - RBK - Teckal Company - Member's Agreement JF PA 2023 (7 Oct 25)
findings.headline: Business model constrained to 80% council-related activity to maintain Teckal compliance
findings.detail: Clause 2.2 requires at least 80% of company activities to be carried out for the council or another council-controlled entity. This Teckal compliance requirement narrows the revenue diversification options and ties the company's viability directly to the council's homelessness demands.
findings.matters: The 80% constraint limits the company's ability to generate alternative revenues or operate commercially. If homelessness demand drops or the council reduces nominations, the company's revenue and debt serviceability are at risk.
findings.figures: 80% of activities must be council-related
findings.quote: at least 80% of the activities of the Company are carried out for or on behalf of the Authority or another person that is controlled by the Authority

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - RBK - Teckal Company - Member's Agreement JF PA 2023 (7 Oct 25)
findings.headline: Council creating a new borrowing entity with no guarantee of council support
findings.detail: The company will be funded by loan capital (clause 6.1) but the council explicitly declines any obligation to provide further finance or guarantee the company's obligations. This creates a standalone debt liability for the new entity, and lenders will need to understand the revenue model (tenancy income from nominated persons).
findings.matters: A new council-controlled borrowing entity changes the council's contingent liabilities picture, even if unguaranteed. Lenders need visibility of the Business Plan to assess whether the company's rental income from homeless persons can service debt without council subsidy.

findings.detail: The council is experiencing higher homelessness approaches than forecast, greater than anticipated losses of PSL properties, and delays in mitigating actions, forcing reliance on expensive Nightly Paid Accommodation (NPA). findings.headline: The council is deferring external borrowing and using internal cash reserves, a strategy that depends on rates remaining manageable
findings.detail: The council has £241.66m of internal borrowing (using cash reserves instead of external borrowing) against £327.4m of external debt. The paper explicitly states this approach 'will require ongoing monitoring if further upside risk to gilt yields prevails,' indicating the strategy is contingent on interest rates not rising significantly beyond current forecasts.
findings.matters: If rates remain elevated or rise further, the council may need to resume external borrowing at higher costs or see its internal cash reserves depleted faster than planned, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £241.66m internal borrowing, £327.4m external debt, £569.05m capital financing requirement
findings.quote: In recent times, the Council has been deferring external borrowing where possible while interest rates are at elevated levels, and has instead been using internal investment balances in lieu of external borrowing (internal borrowing). This is a prudent and cost-effective approach in the current economic climate but will require ongoing monitoring if further upside risk to gilt yields prevails.

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring Report as at Month 4 (31 July 2025)
findings.headline: Cambridge Road Estate Phase 1C delayed due to Building Safety Regulator approvals
findings.detail: The council's major housing development, Cambridge Road Estate, has seen Phase 1C commencement delayed due to additional work needed to secure Building Safety Regulator approvals. This has resulted in underspends of £5.80m across three budget categories (Homeloss/Disturbance £0.56m, CRE Offsite Leaseholder £0.98m, CRE purchase of Affordable Homes £4.26m) that have been reprofiled. The council is also acquiring 55 additional homes from Cambridge Road Estate LLP (£20.54m capital bid, subject to GLA grant approval).
findings.matters: Building Safety Regulator delays are outside the council's direct control but signal either complexity in the development or regulator caution. For a lender, this affects both the timing of asset delivery and the council's capital financing position. The additional property acquisition is also subject to GLA grant which is not yet confirmed.
findings.figures: £5.80m underspend (Phase 1C delays); £4.26m underspend on affordable homes purchase; £20.54m new capital bid for 55 property acquisitions (subject to GLA grant)
findings.quote: commencement of Phase 1C remains delayed owing to the additional work needed to secure Building Safety Regulator approvals... resulting in underspends across three budget categories

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring Report as at Month 4 (31 July 2025)
findings.headline: Capital programme reprofiled by £54.55m from 2025/26 to future years, indicating delivery delays
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme has forecast an in-year underspend of £38.22m with £54.55m being reprofiled across the 4-year programme to later years (2026/27-2028/29). Major delays include Property programmes (£24.65m underspend) still in design or awaiting planning consent, Cambridge Road acquisitions delayed pending Building Safety Regulator approvals (£5.14m underspend), and Housing General Fund temporary accommodation delayed (£3.18m underspend).
findings.matters: Large reprofiling at month 4 signals that original delivery plans were unrealistic. This is a pattern concern: if the council cannot deliver against plan in year 1, it raises questions about project management and planning certainty. Lenders may view this as evidence of weaker delivery capability.
findings.figures: £54.55m reprofiled from 2025/26; £38.22m in-year General Fund underspend; £24.65m Property underspend; £5.14m Cambridge Road underspend
findings.quote: A review is underway across the programme to ensure that all financial commitments are accurately forecast against the delivery plan for each project. As a result, savings on the programme of £9.28m have been identified alongside the rephasing of £45.27m into later years

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring Report as at Month 4 (31 July 2025)
findings.headline: Parking enforcement income shortfall of £0.92m due to 17% drop in visits and industrial action
findings.detail: Parking Enforcement accounts show a £0.31m shortfall overall on Resources. On-street parking income is short by £0.92m. Visits are down 17% compared to Q1 2024/25, and industrial action by civil enforcement officers has reduced income further. Moving traffic enforcement brought in £0.26m and Bus Lane PCN £0.35m, partially offsetting the losses.
findings.matters: Parking income is volatile and demand-driven. A 17% drop in visits suggests either reduced traffic, reduced enforcement capacity, or behavioural change. Industrial action adds a labour stability risk. This income shortfall was not recovered by Month 4.
findings.figures: £0.92m on-street parking shortfall; visits down 17% vs Q1 2024/25; £0.26m moving traffic enforcement gain; £0.35m Bus Lane PCN gain
