findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring Report as at Month 4 (31 July 2025)
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £1.2m due to homecare demand and complexity
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is reporting a £1.2m adverse variance. The council is supporting more people to stay at home longer rather than move into residential care, and the complexity of people's needs being supported at home is requiring more hours of homecare support. Mental health and learning disability spending continues to be challenging due to increased numbers and complexity of need, as well as market pressures increasing costs.
findings.matters: Homecare cost inflation and demographic demand (ageing population) are structural drivers. This is a pattern seen across councils nationally and signals sustained budget pressure. Kingston's population grew 5% 2011-2021 with ageing trends.
findings.figures: £1.2m overspend; population grew 5% between 2011-2021; ageing population trend
findings.quote: Adults Social Care (ASC) continues to face ongoing demand and cost pressures. This has been characterised by an increase in homecare spend as the Council supports more people to stay at home longer

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring Report as at Month 4 (31 July 2025)
findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £1.29m driven by complexity and cost of specialist care placements
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecasting a £1.29m overspend. The budget relating to children in care is forecast to overspend by £0.83m due to rising costs of specialist care placements. Although the number of children in care remains stable (103 vs 101 when budget was set), the complexity of needs is increasing, leading to a higher proportion requiring specialist residential care. S75 health budgets are also overspending (£0.40m) due to unrealistic funding relative to staff pay awards.
findings.matters: Rising placement costs with stable numbers signal either market-driven cost inflation or shifting case complexity. This is a demand pressure that cannot be turned off quickly without risking safeguarding. The council cannot simply reduce numbers of children in care.
findings.figures: £1.29m overspend; £0.83m overspend on specialist care placements; 103 children in care (vs 101 budgeted); £0.40m S75 health overspend
findings.quote: the complexity of children's needs is increasing leading to a higher proportion requiring specialist residential care

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring Report as at Month 4 (31 July 2025)
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation overspend of £0.78m due to higher demand and expensive nightly paid placements
findings.detail: Community Housing is forecasting a £0.78m overspend, predominantly from Temporary Accommodation. The council is facing higher than forecast approaches from homeless households and is relying more heavily on expensive nightly paid accommodation rather than private sector leased property. The service had estimated needing £6m growth but is targeting £3.3m in mitigations; the current position suggests additional TA expenditure of £3.5m versus 2024/25.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a cost signal for homelessness pressure and often reflects both structural housing shortages and economic stress. A lender needs to understand whether this is a one-off spike or structural. The council's mitigation is running behind plan.
findings.figures: £0.78m overspend; £3.5m additional TA expenditure versus 2024/25; initial growth estimate £6m with £3.3m mitigation target
findings.quote: the majority of this overspend relating to Temporary Accommodation as a result of a higher than forecast number of approaches from homeless households and a greater than forecast reliance on more expensive Nightly Paid Accommodation over Private Sector Leased property

findings.paper_title: Revenue & Capital Budget Monitoring Report as at Month 4 (31 July 2025)
findings.headline: High Needs Block (schools) overspending by £10.76m with cumulative DSG deficit rising to £18.73m
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £10.76m (including £1.05m contingency for future demand). The number of EHCPs has increased by 87 since March 2025 to 2,072. The cumulative DSG deficit is forecast to rise from £8.27m at March 2025 to £18.73m by the end of 2025/26. The council acknowledges uncertainty due to timing of new academic year cohorts.
findings.matters: High Needs deficits are structural and cannot be easily turned off. The DSG is technically 'ring-fenced' from the General Fund by statutory override until March 2028, but growing deficits signal rising demand for specialist education that the funding settlement does not cover. This is a long-term fiscal risk.
findings.figures: £10.76m overspend (including £1.05m contingency); 87 net new EHCPs; cumulative deficit rising to £18.73m; 2,072 total EHCPs
findings.quote: The High Needs Block is projected to overspend by £10.76m including £1.05m contingency for future demand... The number of EHCPs has increased by a net 87 since 31 March 2025 to 2,072.

news_drafts.headline: Kingston schools deficit reaches £38m despite government grant
news_drafts.lead: Kingston's schools are facing a £38.72m funding deficit by year-end, driven by rising demand for special educational needs support. The council expects to spend £235.61m on schools against £219.23m in government funding — an £18.18m shortfall this year. The high needs part of school funding, which supports children with special educational needs and disabilities, faces an £18.42m overspend. The council has 2,236 pupils with Education and Health Care Plans, up 8 per cent year-on-year, but government funding has remained frozen. The government has introduced a High Needs Stability Grant to write off 90 per cent of the prior-year deficit (£20.52m), though it has indicated that future support "will not be unlimited".

news_drafts.headline: Kingston pension fund faces software crisis blocking legal deadline
news_drafts.lead: Kingston upon Thames's pension fund is racing against a 1 January 2028 statutory deadline to recalculate benefits for 3,483 members under a legally required reform, but faces a critical software dependency with no confirmed delivery dates. The core system was delivered in July 2025 but defects prevent accurate benefit calculations. The supplier has said patches will fix the issue, but dates remain unconfirmed. Officers rate this a red risk (the highest level) because the work cannot proceed without the patches. The council is using a standalone calculator to ensure members retiring or dying immediately have correct benefits calculated while waiting. The delay stems from industry-wide defects affecting multiple public sector pension funds pressing suppliers for fixes.
